FILE: (African Union 1981) African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights
LAW: African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights
LAWTYPE: 1. Only adds new law to regulatory regime.
LAWJUSTIFY_TXT: The African States members of the Organization of African Unity, parties to the present convention entitled "African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights", Recalling Decision 115 (XVI) of the Assembly of Heads of State and Government at its Sixteenth Ordinary Session held in Monrovia, Liberia, from 17 to 20 July 1979 on the preparation of a "preliminary draft on an African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights providing inter alia for the establishment of bodies to promote and protect human and peoples' rights"; Considering the Charter of the Organization of African Unity, which stipulates that "freedom, equality, justice and dignity are essential objectives for the achievement of the legitimate aspirations of the African peoples"; Reaffirming the pledge they solemnly made in Article 2 of the said Charter to eradicate all forms of colonialism from Africa, to coordinate and intensify their cooperation and efforts to achieve a better life for the peoples of Africa and to promote international cooperation having due regard to the Charter of the United Nations. and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; Taking into consideration the virtues of their historical tradition and the values of African civilization which should inspire and characterize their reflection on the concept of human and peoples' rights; Recognizing on the one hand, that fundamental human rights stem from the attributes of human beings which justifies their national and international protection and on the other hand that the reality and respect of peoples rights should necessarily guarantee human rights; Considering that the enjoyment of rights and freedoms also implies the performance of duties on the part of everyone; Convinced that it is henceforth essential to pay a particular attention to the right to development and that civil and political rights cannot be dissociated from economic, social and cultural rights in their conception as well as universality and that the satisfaction of economic, social and cultural rights ia a guarantee for the enjoyment of civil and political rights; Conscious of their duty to achieve the total liberation of Africa, the peoples of which are still struggling for their dignity and genuine independence, and undertaking to eliminate colonialism, neo-colonialism, apartheid, zionism and to dismantle aggressive foreign military bases and all forms of discrimination, particularly those based on race, ethnic group, color, sex. language, religion or political opinions; Reaffirming their adherence to the principles of human and peoples' rights and freedoms contained in the declarations, conventions and other instrument adopted by the Organization of African Unity, the Movement of Non-Aligned Countries and the United Nations; FILE: BO2010_Ley Contra el Racismo y Toda Forma de Discriminación_SP
LAW: Law Against Racism And All Forms Of Discrimination
LAWTYPE: 4. Adds new law and amends other law(s).
LAWJUSTIFY_TXT: With  the  promulgation  of  the  Political  Constitution  of  the  State,  the  country  began  a  process  of  structural  refoundation,  which  in  the   normative  system  implies  building  a  decolonized  legal  system,  which  repairs  the  evils  generated  by  the  liberal  regulations  that  governed   the  administration  of  justice  for  the  privilege  of  a  few  to  the  detriment  of  many  social  groups.  Now,  the  Political  Constitution  of  the  State  recognizes  the  rights  of  the  country's  social  groups,  incorporating  gender  language  that   equates  Bolivian  men  and  women  in  conditions,  therefore,  the  defense  of  the  rights  of  the  population  requires  a  renovation  of  protection   mechanisms,  coercion,  sanction  and  reparation  in  the  face  of  the  usurpation  of  the  same,  in  such  a  way  that  the  various  fundamental   norms  promulgated,  within  the  framework  of  the  new  vision  of  the  Bolivian  legal  system,  are  urgently  accompanied  by  a  Penal  Reform,   which  is  also  imperative,  by  virtue  of  international  human  rights  law,  particularly  in  the  elimination  of  all  forms  of  discrimination,  respect   for  the  rights  of  indigenous  peoples,  equality  and  equity  of  gender  and  generation,  reasons  why  Bolivia  is  settling  its  pending  debts  with   human  rights  by  adapting  the  Penal  Code  and  the  Code  of  Criminal  Procedure.  The  legal  modifications  made  to  date  by  the  Plurinational  Legislative  Assembly,  in  the  Criminal  Normative  System,  which  assist  in  the  decolonization  process,  are  also  instruments  to  seek  to  establish  the  conditions  of  a  less   unjust  society,  said  normative  modifications  are  carried  out  despite  conservative  and  stubborn  sectors who  seek  to  save  themselves  from  disempowerment,  who  refuse  to  assume  their  responsibilities  and  answer   for  their  actions  in  order  to  protect  themselves  from  impunity.  Faced  with  new  legal  challenges,  the  Ministry  of  Justice  cannot  remain  indifferent  to  the  Bolivian  population,   which  makes  it  necessary  to  socialize  the  modifications  to  the  Criminal  Normative  System,  which  toughen   the  sanctions  against  repeat  offenders,  avoiding  the  delay  of  justice  and  balancing  the  rights  of  the  accused   and  accusers,  preventing  the  accused  from  invoking  precautionary  measures  and  aimed  at  compensating   the  victims  of  crimes  for  damages,  as  well  as  establishing  greater  protection  for  victims  of  crimes.  These   measures,  although  they  have  been  developed  by  state  bodies,  are  the  result  of  the  request  of  the  Bolivian   people,  who  seek  to  broadly  ensure  citizen  security  and  transparency  in  the  administration  of  justice   accompanied  by  intense  action  in  the  fight  against  corruption  throughout  the  country.  However,  it  is  necessary  to  point  out  that  the  modifications  made  to  the  Penal  Code  and  the  Code  of  Criminal   Procedure  will  not  last  over  time;  it  is  the  task  of  each  and  every  Bolivian  to  advocate  for  an  increasingly   perfectible  legal  system  that  responds  to  the  requirements  of  a  developing  society,  with  new  paradigms,  in   the  vision  of  a  new  State

LAWTYPE: 2. Only amends existing law(s) of regime.
LAWJUSTIFY_TXT: That El Salvador recognizes the human person as the origin and the end of the activity of the State, and it is its obligation to ensure that the inhabitants enjoy freedom, legal security, and the common good, as well as the protection and preservation of the right to life, and the physical and moral integrity of individuals, in accordance with Articles 1 and 2 of the Constitution.  II. That through Legislative Decree No. 1030, dated April 26, 1997, published in Official Gazette No. 105, Volume 335, on June 10 of the same year, the Penal Code was approved, which regulates, among other things, crimes related to public order.  III. That in order to fulfill the duties of the State regarding the protection and preservation of these rights, and in light of the increase in criminal activity, the Legislative Assembly, at the initiative of the President of the Republic through the Council of Ministers, issued Legislative Decree No. 333 dated March 27, 2022, published in Official Gazette No. 62, Volume No. 434 on the same date, which establishes the State of Exception. Its purpose is to provide legal tools and mechanisms to public security institutions—the National Civil Police and the Armed Forces of El Salvador—with the aim of restoring public order and citizen security, as well as territorial control.  IV. That due to the excessive increase in violent acts throughout the national territory by criminal structures known as maras or gangs, the lives and integrity of all citizens have been put at risk, creating a situation of alarm, social instability, and widespread fear among the population by imminently endangering people's physical and mental well-being.  V. That it is a well-known fact that the aforementioned criminal organizations systematically carry out attacks against the lives, safety, and personal integrity of the population—including civil, military, police, and penitentiary authorities; against property, through crimes such as extortion of individuals and legal entities; violations of every citizen's right to reside anywhere in the country; attacks against the right to education by forcing students to drop out; against freedom of movement by paralyzing public transportation services nationwide, and often targeting public transportation personnel; and they hinder the free exercise of economic and labor activities across broad sectors of the population—among many other actions carried out in a systematic, planned, and organized manner. VI. That pursuant to the Constitutional Court ruling 22-2007 AC, issued at fifteen hours and twenty-two minutes on August 24, 2015, the criminal structures known as maras or gangs were declared as follows:  "...The gangs known as Mara Salvatrucha or MS-13 and the 18th Street Gang or Mara 18, and any other gang or criminal organization that seeks to usurp the powers inherent to the sovereignty of the State—e.g., territorial control, as well as the monopoly on the legitimate use of force by the institutions that make up the criminal justice system—by instilling fear, gravely endangering, or systematically and indiscriminately violating the fundamental rights of the population or parts of it, are terrorist groups. Therefore, their leaders, members, collaborators, apologists, and financiers are included under the concept of 'terrorists,' in all degrees and forms of participation, regardless of whether such armed groups or criminal organizations have political, criminal, economic (extortion, money laundering, drug trafficking, etc.), or other purposes."  VII. That the maras or gangs, within their organized structures, have the active collaboration of members from various groups, who directly participate in the commission of serious criminal acts, such as homicides, extortion, rape, drug trafficking, illicit associations, terrorist acts, among others. These acts endanger the most fundamental legal rights protected by the Constitution of the Republic, including life, property, liberty, legal security, peace, and national sovereignty.  VIII. That Article 6 of the Constitution recognizes freedom of expression as a fundamental right of every person to express, without undue interference from the State or individuals, their ideas, opinions, and judgments, whether spoken, written, or through any other medium, as a guarantee of all free, pluralistic, and open societies. It is an essential component of the State in the pursuit of a democratic and representative government. However, the exercise of this right is limited insofar as it does not subvert public order.  IX–X. THEREFORE, that currently, the terrorist structures known as maras or gangs, with the aim of exercising territorial control over specific areas, use language techniques such as graffiti, texts, paintings, designs, drawings, or any form of visual expression freely created on public and private infrastructure. These are intended to convey messages of threat, death, or restrictions on freedom, causing a negative impact on the population and directly affecting public order. Such expressions constitute mechanisms that support the actions of these terrorist groups.  That in light of the illegitimate exercise of the right to freedom of expression by terrorist organizations—maras or gangs—it is necessary to expand the catalog of crimes committed by all members, collaborators, apologists, and financiers of these groups. The goal is to repress and deter individuals from engaging in legally prohibited behavior, so that knowing the negative consequences of a particular act, they refrain from violating the legal order.

LAWJUSTIFY_TXT: That the Constitution of the Republic establishes in its Articles 1 and 2 that El Salvador recognizes the human person as the origin and the end of the activity of the State, which is organized to achieve justice, legal security, and the common good, as well as the preservation of the right to life, and the physical and moral integrity of individuals.  That through Legislative Decree No. 349, dated April 5, 2022, published in Official Gazette No. 69, Volume No. 435, on April 5, 2022, the Penal Code was amended to incorporate Article 345-C, which, in its second paragraph, established that a criminal offense would be committed by anyone who, through the use of Information and Communication Technologies, radio, television, written or digital media, reproduces and transmits messages or communications originating or allegedly originating from criminal groups that could generate anxiety and panic among the general population.  That currently, the State, through the security measures it has implemented—specifically the execution of the Territorial Control Plan and the State of Exception approved by this Legislative Assembly—has responded effectively and immediately to the criminal actions of terrorist groups, through territorial interventions and the establishment of security perimeters. This has succeeded in dismantling their operations, fulfilling the objectives of security policies, and preventing the dissemination of all types of messages that represented threats, death, or restrictions on the population’s freedom.  In addition, various sectors of society, including the general population, have regained trust in the authorities and are actively reporting the actions of terrorist groups, which has made the functions of public security institutions even more effective, thereby consolidating the results achieved in the effort to eradicate the actions of these criminal groups.  That in accordance with Article 6 of the Constitution, which states in its first paragraph that “Every person may freely express and disseminate their thoughts provided they do not subvert public order, or offend morality, honor, or the private life of others…,” this Assembly considers it necessary to reaffirm the exercise of the right to freedom of expression, as the effectiveness of public security policies and the decisive actions taken by the State to halt the spread of messages that generated fear in the population have been clearly demonstrated. These results have been achieved through coordinated work among institutions and without persecuting or undermining in any way the work of the media.
